units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Dyna-Q: Learning from Imagined Steps

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Remember what happened, then replay those memories to learn faster.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Q-learning uses each real step once, then throws it away. Dyna-Q also writes each real step into a model: a table of "here, this move, gave this reward and led there". After every real step it replays a few remembered steps from the model through the same Q-learning update. The reward found at the charging dock spreads back across the floor in a few trips instead of many. The model must stay right: if the floor changes, stale memories mislead the robot.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 1. One real step feeds two things at once. It teaches the score directly, and the same step is written into the memory of steps, from which remembered steps rise back into learning. So one real step teaches twice, once directly and once through replay.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Figure 1 shows one real step feeding two things at once. The green arrow is the real step, which teaches the score directly, and the same step is written into the memory of steps, from which dashed remembered steps rise back into learning. Take the step onto the dock: it teaches the score for that step and is stored, so later replays can teach from it again without a new real step.

units.spoken: The running example is the warehouse robot again, on a floor laid out like the maze in Sutton and Barto's book.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: A few short rows of shelving racks stand on the floor as walls.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: The robot starts in the start bay, on the left edge of the floor, and the dock sits in the far corner.

units.spoken: 1.2 The agent, its state, its moves and its reward

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: Here the robot is the agent, the learner that picks the moves. The floor is a grid of cells, and each move takes the robot one cell.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: A state is the situation the robot stands in right now. A move, or action, is one choice it can make in that state. A reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: A real step is one move made in the real world, with the reward and the next state it brings.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: On this floor the racks block the way. The book's maze has no ledge, no edge the robot can fall off: steps cost nothing, and only reaching the dock pays.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: 1.3 One trip, its return, and the Q-table

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: Each run from the start to the dock is one episode, also called a trip.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: In the book's maze the first trips wander a long time before the robot finds it.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: Because later rewards count a little less, the dock is worth more when it is reached sooner, so short routes win.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: A move's value Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes move a in state s and plays on from there. A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move.

units.section: 1 Each real experience is used once
units.spoken: Each score is the robot's current guess of that move's value Q of s and a; after each real step, the update nudges the stored score of the move just made toward what the step showed.

The robot sits in the cell beside the dock, the one square the real step must light. One real step lights only that cell, and the cells behind stay dark until the robot walks them again.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: When it works, the robot can learn from a step without taking it again.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: A model is the agent's learned guess of where a move leads and what it pays. Planning means using a model to try moves in imagination instead of in the real world.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: On this floor the same move from the same cell always gives the same result, so one entry per cell and move is enough.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: These written-down steps fill the box "memory of steps", and real and remembered steps both feed the box "learn from it".

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps

units.spoken: 2.1 Replay a remembered step

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: The planning step: replay through the same update

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: Picture the robot replaying a step it already took, without moving. A Dyna planning step replays a remembered step through the same Q-learning update, as if it happened again.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: Pick a cell and move already tried, look up the reward and next cell, and nudge that score. The number of imagined steps per real step is written n plan; the book writes n.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: When it works, the dock reward spreads back at most n plan plus one cells per real step instead of one.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 3. One imagined replay carries the score one cell further back. The dock sits at the top, the cell beside it is lit, and the dashed arrow carries the score down to the next cell back, which lights too. Replaying the step that starts two cells back and lands on the lit cell lifts its score, so the reward spreads one cell further without a new real step.

units.spoken: Figure 3 follows one imagined replay as it carries the score one cell further back. The dock sits at the top, the cell beside it is lit, and the dashed arrow carries the score down to the next cell back, which lights too. Take the cell two back from the dock, the one the arrow reaches: replaying the step that starts there and lands on the lit cell beside the dock lifts its score, so the reward spreads one cell further without a new real step.

units.spoken: 2.2 Real moves stay epsilon-greedy

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: Epsilon-greedy usually plays the top-scored move and, with chance epsilon, a random one instead.

units.section: 2 Remembering and replaying steps
units.spoken: The robot picks every real move this way. The random moves keep it trying new cells instead of repeating its best move so far.

sections.section: 3 The Q update and the model update

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Section three, The Q update and the model update

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Q-learning's target is the step's reward plus the discounted best score in the next state. Bootstrapping means putting your own current guess for the next state inside the target.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: On a planning step the model supplies the guess of the next cell from its remembered landing cell, so the discounted best score serves real and remembered steps alike.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The TD (temporal difference) error delta is how much one step surprised the agent, the target minus the current guess. The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: 3.1 Aim, measure, nudge

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The Q update: the score learns from one real step

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Picture the score for one move moving toward what the step showed. The Q update aims at the target, measures the surprise, and nudges the score.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The target is the step's reward plus the discounted best score from the next cell. The surprise is the target minus the score, and the score moves a learning-rate share of the surprise.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: When it works, the score closes part of the gap on each step.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Equation 1. The Q update. The robot has just stepped from the cell beside the dock onto the dock.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. In four lines, the Q update aims at a target, measures the surprise, and nudges the score part of the way there.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The first line is the target. Y sub t is the target for the step just taken, the value the score should move toward. T counts real steps, so r sub t plus 1 is the reward that follows step t. On this line the target is just the reward, nothing more. On this floor the reward is nothing on every step except the step onto the dock, which pays. So the target is what the score should move toward, and only the dock step pays.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Intuition. The target is what the score should move toward, and on this floor only the step onto the dock pays.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The mathematics. y sub t equals r sub t plus 1 plus gamma times the best score from the cell the robot reached. y sub t is the target for the step just taken, the value the score should move toward. t counts real steps, so r sub t plus 1 is the reward that follows step t. On this floor r sub t plus 1 is nothing on every step except the step onto the dock, which pays.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Example. Take the step onto the dock: it pays, and the score for that step moves toward the reward.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The second line is the future score. The plus adds the future score to the reward the step just brought in. Gamma is the discount, how much a reward one step later still counts, and it stands next to the best score with nothing between them, which means multiply. Max over a takes the best score over every move. Q of s sub t plus 1 and a is the best score from the cell the robot reached. At the dock the trip ends and this line is left out, so the target is the reward alone. The best score from the next cell is what the future is worth.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Intuition. The best score from the next cell is what the future is worth.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The mathematics. This line says plus gamma times the max over a of Q of s sub t plus 1 and a. The plus adds the future score to the reward r sub t plus 1, the payoff the step just brought in. gamma is the discount, how much a reward one step later still counts, and it stands next to the best score with nothing between them, which means multiply. Max over a takes the best over every move a. Q of s sub t plus 1 and a is the best score from the cell the robot reached. At the dock the trip ends and this line is left out, so the target is the reward alone.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Example. Take the cell beside the dock: its best move leads onto the dock, so the discounted best score from there is already high.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The third line is the surprise. Delta sub t is the TD error, the target minus the current guess. Y sub t is the target, the reward plus the discounted best score from the next cell. Q of s sub t and a sub t is the score of the move a sub t just played in the cell s sub t. The minus takes the guess away from the target, so delta sub t is positive when the step turned out better than the score said, negative when worse, and zero when the score was exactly right. So the surprise is the gap between the target and the score as it stands.
termList: Q of s sub t and a sub t

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Intuition. The surprise is the gap between the target and the score as it stands.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The mathematics. delta sub t equals y sub t minus Q of s sub t and a sub t. delta sub t is the TD error, the target minus the current guess. y sub t is the target, the reward r sub t plus 1 plus the discounted best score from the next cell. Q of s sub t and a sub t is the score of the move a sub t just played in the cell s sub t. The minus takes the guess away from the target, so delta sub t is positive when the step turned out better than the score said, negative when worse, and zero when the score was exactly right.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Example. Take the step onto the dock: the score said little, the step pays well, so the error is large and positive.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The fourth line is the nudge. Q of s sub t and a sub t on the left is the new score, and the arrow means replace with. Q of s sub t and a sub t on the right is the old score, the one the step started from, and only the entry for the cell and move just played is nudged. The plus adds eta times delta sub t. Eta is the learning rate, the share of the surprise the score takes in, and delta sub t is the TD error, target minus guess. The score moves only part of the way toward its target.
termList: Q of s sub t and a sub t

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Intuition. The score moves only part of the way toward its target.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The mathematics. Q of s sub t and a sub t on the left is the new score, and the arrow reads replace with. Q of s sub t and a sub t on the right is the old score, the one the step started from, and only the entry for the cell and move just played is nudged. The plus adds eta times delta sub t: eta is the learning rate, the share of the surprise the score takes in, and delta sub t is the TD error, target minus guess. Q of s sub t and a sub t gets replaced by Q of s sub t and a sub t plus eta times delta sub t. So the whole equation says this: aim at the target the step earned, measure the surprise, and nudge the score part of the way there.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Example. Take the score for stepping north onto the dock: it rises by a learning-rate share of the surprise, not all the way to the target.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Take the robot in the cell beside the dock, stepping north onto the dock. The step pays and the trip ends there, so the error is large, and the score for stepping north moves a learning-rate share toward it. A step landing one cell short pays nothing, but the best score from the cell it reached stays high.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The book writes alpha for the learning rate.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: 3.2 Store, recall, imagine

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The model update: the score learns from one remembered step

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Picture the model table handing back a step it stored. The model update stores the step, recalls a pair, a tried cell and its move, builds an imagined target, and nudges the recalled score.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Store the reward and next cell under the cell and move. Recall a tried pair, build its imagined target from the remembered reward and the discounted best score, and nudge the recalled score the same way.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: When it works, learning from remembered steps uses the same rule as learning from real ones, so each real step teaches many times over.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Equation 2. The model. One real step teaches one cell. The model is how the robot keeps learning from steps it already took, without taking new ones.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. In four lines, the model stores each real step, recalls a tried pair, builds an imagined target, and nudges the recalled score.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The first line is the store. Model of s sub t and a sub t is the table entry for the cell s sub t and the move a sub t just played. The arrow means store as: the entry is set to the pair on the right. The pair on the right holds two things: r sub t plus 1, the reward the real floor paid for that move, and s sub t plus 1, the next cell it landed in. The model is the table of remembered steps, one entry per cell and move tried. So one real step is written down so it can be replayed later.

units.spoken: Intuition. One real step is written down so it can be replayed later.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The mathematics. Model of s sub t and a sub t gets stored as the pair r sub t plus 1 and s sub t plus 1. Model of s sub t and a sub t is the table entry for the cell s sub t and the move a sub t just played. The arrow reads store as: the entry is set to the pair on the right. The pair r sub t plus 1 and s sub t plus 1 is two things at once: r sub t plus 1 is the reward the real floor paid for that move, and s sub t plus 1 is the next cell it landed in. The model is the table of remembered steps, one entry per cell and move tried.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: Example. Take the step north onto the dock: the model stores that it paid and ended on the dock.

units.section: 3 The Q update and the model update
units.spoken: The second line is the recall. The pair r hat and s hat next are the remembered reward and the remembered next cell. Model of s tilde and a tilde looks them up in the table for the cell s tilde and move a tilde picked at random from those already tried. The small mark above a letter is a hat, and it marks a guess from the model, not the floor. The wavy mark is a tilde, and it marks a cell and a move already tried. Between real steps the robot replays a move it already tried.

units.spoken: Example. Take a move made two cells back: the model returns its remembered reward and next cell without a new real step.

units.spoken: Section four, Stepping through one Dyna-Q step

units.section: 4 Stepping through one Dyna-Q step
units.spoken: The walkthrough starts mid-training, so the model table already holds a few steps. One step runs seven stages: a real step, its target, its update, the remembered step, a recall, a replay, then a new real step.

units.section: 4 Stepping through one Dyna-Q step
units.spoken: Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run one Dyna-Q step through its seven stages, or step through it with Next. Stage one takes a real step, stage two builds its target, stage three updates its score, stage four stores the step, stage five recalls a step tried before, stage six replays it, and stage seven takes a new real step. The equation card lights the line each stage uses. Press Reset to start the walk again.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: Section five, One Dyna-Q step in code

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: One Dyna-Q step on the warehouse floor. Env step of s and a is the real floor; it returns the reward, the next cell and whether the robot reached the dock.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: This code sets up the floor and the two tables. It makes a floor 6 by 9, sets the learning rate to 0.1, the discount to 0.95, exploration to 0.1, and five imagined steps per real step. The Q-table starts at zero and the model starts empty, and the robot starts in the start bay. So the run starts with two empty tables and one starting cell.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: 1. The setup: the Q-table starts at zero and the model starts empty.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: This code is the real floor. It takes a cell and a move, works out the next cell, and holds the robot in place when the move hits a wall or leaves the floor. A move onto the dock pays 1 and ends the trip; any other move pays nothing. So the floor is simple: walls block, and the dock pays.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: 2. The real floor: a move into a wall or off the floor stays put; a move onto the dock pays and ends the trip.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: This code takes one real step. It picks a move by epsilon-greedy: a random move with chance epsilon, else the top-scored move, with ties broken at random. It takes the step, builds the target from the reward plus the discounted best score, zero at the dock, and nudges the score by the learning rate times the surprise. That is the whole update: aim, measure, nudge.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: 3. The Q update equation: the target, the surprise, and the nudge.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: This code remembers the step. It stores the reward, the next cell and whether the trip ended under the cell and move just played, then moves to the next cell. So the model holds one entry per cell and move.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: 4. The model equation: store the step as its reward and next cell.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: This code plans. It replays five imagined steps: each time it picks a tried cell at random, picks a tried move from it, looks up the remembered reward and next cell, builds the imagined target, and nudges the recalled score. So planning is the same update, run on remembered steps.

units.section: 5 One Dyna-Q step in code
units.spoken: 5. The model equation: recall a step, build its imagined target, and nudge its score, n plan times.

sections.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps

units.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps
units.spoken: Section six, Fewer real steps with more imagined steps

units.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps
units.spoken: The run below covers the first few hundred real steps after the first trip. It uses learning rate 0.1, discount 0.95, exploration 0.1, and zero, five or fifty imagined steps per real step, on a floor 6 by 9. The book's figure averages 30 runs; the tool shows one run per setting with a fixed seed, a starting number that fixes the randomness so the same run repeats. Every setting behaves the same until the first trip, so the step count starts after it. Within this run, more imagined steps per real step carry the dock's reward back in fewer real steps.

units.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 4. More imagined steps means fewer real steps. The maze shades each square by its score with the gold route over it, and the bars show when a route forms for each setting. By the end of this run, imagined steps have formed a route; without them, no route forms within the run. Imagined steps cost computing, and they save real steps.

units.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps
units.spoken: Try the tool. The top slider sets the imagined steps after each real one, and the lower slider sets the real steps since the first trip. Watch the maze shade by score as the gold route forms, and watch the bars show when each setting forms it. Set the top slider to five imagined steps and the lower slider much later in the run, and the readout says a route has formed. With no imagined steps, it says the score spread back only to the cell beside the dock.

units.section: 6 Fewer real steps with more imagined steps
units.spoken: Figure 4 shows how imagined steps trade against real steps on the maze. The top slider sets the imagined steps after each real one, the lower slider sets the real steps since the first trip, the maze shades each square by its score with the gold route over it, and the bars show when a route forms for each setting. The dashed line marks the real step the lower slider has reached. Set the top slider to five imagined steps and the lower slider to much later in the run. The readout says a route has formed. With no imagined steps, it says the score spread back only to the cell beside the dock.

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: Section seven, The robot carries two tables

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: The robot carries two tables: the Q-table of scores and the model table of remembered steps.

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: The model is a dict, a lookup table keyed by cell and move: each entry holds the reward and the next cell that move gave. Planning samples only pairs already seen, and uses the same learning rate for real and imagined updates.

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: With more imagined steps per real step, the agent learns faster from each real step, at the cost of more computing: every imagined step is work the computer does for each real step. Fewer imagined steps keep the run closer to plain Q-learning.

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: 7.1 More imagined steps, fewer trips

units.section: 7 The robot carries two tables
units.spoken: The book's maze has 47 states. Its figure averages 30 runs: with no imagined steps the agent took about 25 episodes to near-optimal, with five imagined steps it took about five episodes, and with fifty imagined steps only three. The first episode took about 1700 steps for every setting.

sections.section: 8 When a table model is enough

units.section: 8 When a table model is enough
units.spoken: Section eight, When a table model is enough

units.section: 8 When a table model is enough
units.spoken: Dyna-Q suits a floor with a small number of cells, rules that are unknown but do not change, and real steps that cost more than imagined steps.

units.section: 8 When a table model is enough
units.spoken: Against Q-learning it reaches the same answer with far fewer real steps.

units.section: 8 When a table model is enough
units.spoken: A Q-network is a neural network that takes the state and outputs one score per move, in place of the table.

units.section: 8 When a table model is enough
units.spoken: The Deep Q-Networks page uses one so it can learn from large inputs such as screens.

sections.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Section nine, When old or lucky memories mislead

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Old or lucky memories: the bonus that re-checks stale moves

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Picture the floor changing while the model still says the old route is best: the short path gets blocked, and a new opening appears elsewhere. A changed floor or a lucky outcome makes replays teach wrong scores.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: The model replays old steps, so it keeps teaching the old route after the floor changes. Dyna-Q+ adds a small bonus in its planning updates for moves not tried for a long time.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: When it works, the robot goes back now and then and re-checks moves it has not tried for a long time, so it finds the new opening. When it fails, replays amplify whatever the model holds, right or wrong.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Equation 3. The Dyna-Q+ bonus. Untried moves get a bonus in planning.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. In one line, untried moves get a bonus in planning, so the robot goes back and re-checks them.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: The one line is the bonus. R plan is the reward the planning update uses, not the remembered reward r. The plus adds the bonus to the remembered reward. Kappa is a small weight in the code, 0.0001 for the blocking maze and 0.001 for the shortcut maze. Tau is the number of real steps since the pair was last tried in a real interaction. The bonus is kappa times the square root of tau. It grows slowly, so the bonus stays small. Raising kappa raises the bonus, so stale moves are re-checked more; lowering it shrinks the bonus. At zero the bonus vanishes, but untried moves are still replayed. So a move not tried for a long time looks better in planning.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Intuition. A move not tried for a long time looks better in planning.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: The mathematics. r plan equals r plus kappa times the square root of tau. r plan is the reward the planning update uses, not the remembered reward r. kappa is a small weight in the code, 0.0001 for the blocking maze and 0.001 for the shortcut maze. tau is the number of real steps since the pair was last tried in a real interaction. The plus adds that bonus to the remembered reward. It grows slowly, so the bonus stays small. Raising kappa raises the bonus, so stale moves are re-checked more; lowering it shrinks the bonus. At zero the bonus vanishes, but untried moves are still replayed, so planning is not plain Dyna-Q; too large and it swamps real rewards.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Example. Take a move not tried for a long time: its planned reward is the remembered reward plus a small bonus.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Blocking maze. The short path gets blocked after 1000 steps. Both Dyna-Q and Dyna-Q+ find the short path within 1000 steps, then the block stops the reward and each agent wanders behind the barrier with no reward for a stretch. When the new opening appears, both agents find the new route after about 800 steps.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Shortcut maze. A shorter path opens along the right side after 3000 steps. Dyna-Q+ finds the shortcut, while plain Dyna-Q never finds it: its model says the old route is best, and the more it plans the less likely it is to take the step to the right and discover the shortcut.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Random outcomes. A table that stores one outcome makes the robot trust a lucky result. The book's Exercise 8.5 asks how the algorithm might be changed for environments where the same move gives different outcomes, without giving the answer. One answer is to store counts of outcomes and sample from them, so a lucky result counts for only its share.

units.section: 9 When old or lucky memories mislead
units.spoken: Many planning steps on a wrong model. Many updates from bad memories drive the scores far from the right values, because each replay teaches the wrong score again.
